title: 121 Years Ago Today, She Swam Faster Than Every Man | Gertrude Ederle

lines: On this day, October 23.
On this day, October twenty-third.
121 years ago today,
One hundred twenty-one years ago today,
a girl was born in New York City.
Many people believed no woman could swim the English Channel.
She did it, and she beat every man who had tried before her.
Her name: Gertrude Ederle.
Her name, Gertrude Ederly.
She was born on October 23, 1905, in New York City.
She was born on October twenty-third, nineteen-oh-five, in New York City.
Her father ran a butcher shop in Manhattan.
She learned to swim in New Jersey,
at a beach where her family spent its summers.
A childhood illness left her with weak hearing,
but in the water, she felt completely at home.
As a teenager, she joined the Women's Swimming Association
and began to set one record after another.

nodes.small: Learning to swim in New Jersey

lines: In 1924, she swam for the United States
In nineteen twenty-four, she swam for the United States
at the Olympic Games in Paris.
She won a gold medal in the relay,
and two bronze medals in her own races.
But she was dreaming of something much bigger:
the English Channel, between France and England.
In 1925, she made her first attempt to cross the Channel.
In nineteen twenty-five, she made her first attempt to cross the Channel.
Halfway across, she was pulled out of the water,
and disqualified on a technicality.
Many people said that was the end of it.
But she did not give up.
She knew she could do it, and she wanted another chance.
She went home, trained harder, and came back a year later.
On the morning of August 6, 1926,
On the morning of August sixth, nineteen twenty-six,
she walked into the sea at Cap Gris-Nez, in France.
She had coated her body with grease to keep out the cold.
The waves were rough, and the weather turned stormy.
Her support boat followed close beside her, all day long.
Hour after hour, she kept swimming, stroke after stroke.
After about fourteen and a half hours,
she came ashore at Kingsdown, in England.
She was the first woman ever to swim the English Channel,
and she beat the men's record by nearly two hours.
Back in New York, huge crowds filled the streets
for a ticker-tape parade in her honour.
Newspapers around the world told her story.
Her swim showed the world what women athletes could do.
She later performed in swimming shows and even appeared in a film.
Her hearing grew worse over the years, until she was almost deaf.
So she spent much of her life teaching deaf children to swim.
She died on November 30, 2003, at the age of ninety-eight.
She died on November thirtieth, two thousand three, at the age of ninety-eight.
They said it could not be done, and she showed them it could.
She did not wait for anyone's permission.
She simply swam, stroke by stroke, all the way to the other side.
And when she lost her hearing, she gave her gift to others.
So here is her question for you:
what are people telling you that you cannot do?
